title: A smart folder? A working approach to organizing project knowledge
text:
Have you ever chatted with your own files? What if that conversation helped you examine not only their contents, but how you were developing the project itself?
That question introduces what I am exploring here. Beyond asking an AI assistant to summarize documents, I am working with a folder that records instructions, sources, discussions, decisions, and current understanding—and makes some relationships among them explicit.
The conversation can then turn toward the work’s development: Where did this interpretation come from? What changed? Which assumptions remain unresolved? What should we revisit next?

title: A smart folder? A working approach to organizing project knowledge
section: From keeping files to preserving relationships
text:
From keeping files to preserving relationships
Folders already help us organize work through filenames, locations, and versions. But reconstructing why something changed often depends on our memory, an email exchange, or a colleague’s explanation.
In this project, I am trying to record selected relationships alongside the files:

A current interpretation points to the discussions and sources behind it.
A decision records its rationale and status.
A session identifies what changed and what remains unresolved.
A project-state record identifies the next work to undertake.

The aim is to make those connections available when returning to the project. Whether the record is sufficient—or too demanding to maintain—remains part of the exploration.

title: A smart folder? A working approach to organizing project knowledge
text:
What travels with the folder?
The workspace carries both project content and guidance for engaging with it.







Element
What it contributes




Working instructions
Explain the project’s purpose, responsibilities, boundaries, and reading order.


Current project state
Identifies open decisions, next actions, and unfinished work.


Session records
Preserve selected discussion, changes in understanding, and unresolved questions.


Decision records
Identify choices, their rationale, and whether they remain active.


Synthesized knowledge
Separates current understanding from the history of its development.


Sources and assessments
Record supporting material, what was checked, and the limits of that reading.


Links and metadata
Connect these records so their relationships can be followed.


Automated checks
Detect specified inconsistencies, such as references to missing sources or sessions.



For example, AGENTS.md tells an assistant how to begin working in this repository, including what to read and which actions require authorization. Those instructions are also readable by a person. They guide work; they do not guarantee compliance.
Likewise, an automated check can establish that a source identifier exists. It cannot establish that the source supports the argument being made.

title: A smart folder? A working approach to organizing project knowledge
text:
What does the conversation add?
An AI assistant can work with the available records to help locate relevant material, compare formulations, identify apparent inconsistencies, and propose revisions.
The interaction becomes more specific when the folder carries an explicit working context. Instead of repeatedly explaining the project from the beginning, I can ask questions such as:

How does this proposal relate to our recorded decisions?


Which parts of this account have been checked, and which remain my interpretation?


What would need updating if we changed this definition?

The assistant’s response still needs review. It may overlook material, misunderstand a relationship, or produce a plausible reconstruction that the records do not support. The files provide grounds for examining its answer.

title: A smart folder? A working approach to organizing project knowledge
section: A small example from this project
text:
A small example from this project
During development of the presentation, we explored several meanings for a symbol in the conceptual model. Through discussion, I accepted a working definition while leaving its foundations and diagrammatic use open for further review.
We then preserved a checkpoint connecting:
Discussion and alternatives considered
                  ↓
Accepted working definition
                  ↓
Updated synthesis and decision record
                  ↓
Questions requiring further review
The checkpoint records a change in the project’s understanding. It does not turn that understanding into a verified claim.
Choosing to preserve that moment also became part of the discussion: I was deciding that this change was consequential enough to record before continuing. The record therefore reflects judgment about what matters, rather than capturing everything that happened.
The October 26 session, current synthesis and decision provide a concrete trail to follow.

title: A smart folder? A working approach to organizing project knowledge
text:
Why “smart”—and why the question mark?
“Smart” describes the arrangement I am exploring: content accompanied by instructions, explicit relationships, and checks that can support further interaction.
It does not mean the folder understands the project. Its usefulness depends on people recording enough context, recognizing errors, and maintaining the connections.
The question mark also reflects a practical difficulty encountered in TAPs development. Preserving interactions and developing knowledge produced an administrative burden that interfered with product work. More documentation was not automatically more useful.
This repository is another attempt to work through that tension. It introduces further questions:

What deserves preservation, and what can be left out?
When does a discussion belong in the current synthesis?
How do we distinguish an accepted decision from a plausible suggestion?
Can another person follow the record without the original conversations?
How much effort does maintaining the structure require?
Which instructions and organizational choices remain appropriate as the project changes?

title: A smart folder? A working approach to organizing project knowledge
text:
Where the work stands
The repository currently contains editable records, working instructions, linked source and session metadata, provenance checks, and browsable project pages. The author retains responsibility for its claims and decisions, and the records remain maintainable without AI.
I will present it as one approach emerging from the work: a response to difficulties in preserving and engaging with developing project knowledge that brings its own choices and demands.
The open question is what this arrangement makes possible in practice—and what we learn about our working approach by trying to use it.

Understanding can remain an intended purpose while the development of representations and the recorded grounds for consequential changes provide a more inspectable object. Working synthesis — GenAI’s role and the proposed contribution
Author-proposed narrative logic (October 22), under development:

Initial understanding and specification. Working from an initial understanding of WRIS, the author developed a dataset specification with GenAI support and reasoning externalization. It appeared coherent and ready to guide a query for a dataset intended for the Oregon Open Data Portal. This describes perceived readiness, not validated readiness; the initial specification remains to be checked.
Learning and challenge. Multiple learning sessions changed the author’s understanding of the records and challenged the initial interpretation and specification. GenAI also supported tracing that evolving understanding. The existing evidence table is the proposed route to checking the sequence and specific revisions.
Revised specification and explanatory artifacts. The author reports an updated structure reflecting the understanding developed through those sessions, together with externalized reasoning artifacts intended to help explain the data source and consequential choices. Dataset publication, final approval, expert consensus, and improved public comprehension are not established by this account.

The assistant recommends referring to the author’s initial understanding rather than generalizing a “naive” view to others. This sequence gives GenAI a role in both the initial formulation and subsequent tracing of revision. A possible interpretive lesson is that coherence and reasoning records require continuing encounters with subject-matter knowledge and evidence. The case does not establish that GenAI caused the initial limitations or that externalization alone produced the revised understanding. Candidate claims WR-01 through WR-03 are registered for evidence review before slide use.
The author describes GenAI’s dual role in this practice: it is a medium for hybrid reasoning and produces externalization artifacts that the user verifies and integrates into a durable project record. Verification and integration are human responsibilities; a generated explanation is not automatically an adequate record. This describes the author’s intended process, not a verified account of every session.
The author identifies two concrete developments from the WRIS learning process: a conceptual-model comparison intended to communicate the changed understanding, and an improved specification for a water-rights dataset intended for the Oregon Open Data Portal. The supplied comparison (local candidate artifacts/talk/assets/water_rights_conceptual_models.png, intentionally untracked pending asset documentation) was visually inspected: it contrasts an assumed single complete record with a representation involving connected record families. The author created it with GenAI assistance and reports a separate document explaining the reasoning and conceptual models behind it; that document has not been inspected here. The image is an explanatory conceptual model, not a validated schema. The initial assumption belongs to this account and should not be attributed to all users. The revised specification, its validation and any publication remain unchecked in this continuation. Improved understanding by planning collaboratives has not been assessed.
Candidate contribution, proposed by the assistant: a situated account of using human-reviewed hybrid reasoning records to support both dataset design and public explanation, including the practical difficulty of sustaining those records. A possible narrative connection is learning encounters → changed understanding → externalized and reviewed reasoning → explanatory artifacts and dataset specifications → opportunities for public examination. This is a provisional account to check, not a demonstrated causal chain or evidence that equitable outcomes followed. The author’s suggested relevance to historical databases across state agencies needs either attribution as a proposed transfer or additional evidence.
For an accessible talk, the conceptual-model comparison is a candidate anchor for the change in understanding, supported by the existing evidence table. Following the author’s subsequent scope constraint, the assistant recommends using the checked Mid-Coast methodological cautions to explain public relevance and leaving the newspaper example out of the talk. Keep the image’s technical assertions subject to the same claim and source checks as prose before slide use.


Proof-of-concept preparation and documentation gap — October 22
The author describes preparing a proof-of-concept website for a quarterly TAPs implementation Working Group meeting, illustrating convergence of groundwater, surface-water, and water-rights data streams into the TAPs product. The group is described as a cross-divisional body coordinating development and confirming milestone readiness, with discussion and documentation required for changes to data structures and processing. These are author-reported organizational arrangements.
As work continued across sessions, documentation accumulated in the main repository. Creating an additional repository for the proof of concept introduced an inter-repository coordination policy and further administrative work. The author ultimately prioritized artifacts over some documentation: session records, AI-session registers, time trackers, and a parallel folder structure fell behind.
The most consequential gap, in the author’s assessment, was the local session record. The conversations reportedly remain in the ChatGPT archive, but loss of access would leave a substantial gap in the locally available account of design choices shaping the proof of concept shared with the group. This is a conditional dependency risk, not a report that the conversations have been lost or that group decision requirements were bypassed.
The transition remains in progress. After the meeting, competing grants-program responsibilities displaced this work, while access to agentic capabilities expanded. The author identifies this repository’s structure, instructions, and record-creation practices as the emerging model informed by that experience. Its effectiveness and transfer to TAPs have not been established. This repository preserves curated session reasoning and decisions rather than raw transcripts. The author clarifies that both approaches serve the same guiding principle of hybrid reasoning externalization; session archiving was a defensive practice, not the defining documentation structure.
The author further clarifies that the explanations and qualifications in the supplied site pages were developed with GenAI assistance while preparing the site. The artifact itself therefore contains reasoning externalization. This does not establish how completely those explanations preserve the earlier development process. A useful distinction for discussion is between the explanation available to a present reader and the record needed to revisit how consequential choices developed.
The author identifies a specific missing rationale: the reasoning behind the framework’s third proposition, which states that SME-mediated interpretation and explicit translation rules are needed to convert heterogeneous WRIS records into defined analytical units. The site states that conclusion and briefly explains the proposed mapping task, but, in the author’s assessment, does not preserve the reasoning that led to recognizing the requirement. The author regards this as one of the most significant developments in understanding how to use and interpret water-rights data. This establishes the author’s identification and assessment of the gap; its underlying reasoning, chronology, and empirical basis remain to be examined. No actual reviewer misunderstanding has been demonstrated.

Public interpretation and planning collaboratives — October 22
Current presentation boundary: the author agrees that the article’s calculations should not be reopened and directs extreme care and minimal use of material needed to support the point. The assistant’s implementation recommendation is to omit the named article, its map, numerical comparisons and analysis of the dispute from the talk, using the Mid-Coast memorandum and the conceptual-model comparison instead. The article assessment below is retained as development provenance, not a proposed public case. This scope boundary supersedes earlier suggestions to use the article as the public-stakes example; it does not settle a complete slide sequence.
The author emphasizes that the understanding behind WRIS translation must be communicable to the public, especially planning collaboratives. The intended relevance extends to how people interpret and use the published data, beyond internal review and maintenance. Avoiding controversial interpretations is an author-stated concern; the effectiveness of any communication practice has not been demonstrated.
The author identifies the existing wris-from-data-structure evidence table as the reconstruction of the reasoning behind the need for SME-mediated translation. The talk can draw on a bounded account checked against that table without requiring the audience to follow the technical reconstruction. The table’s underlying passages still require checking before public claims are promoted.
The supplied 2016 article registered as draining-oregon-2016 provides a possible public-context example. Its map compares permitted withdrawals with estimated replenishment; the text reports disagreement about that comparison and distinguishes authorization from actual pumping. It supports discussion of contested public inference, but does not establish the author’s stronger assessment that the analysis lacked understanding of WRIS structure or SME translation. Methods, data extraction, record handling and underlying responses remain unchecked. The supplied file is a WaterWatch republication, not a checked original methods package. Keep the source’s published claims, the author’s critique and the assistant’s limited assessment distinct.
Candidate extension of the contribution, proposed by the assistant: make the basis and limits of data interpretation available to people who will use and question the products, including planning collaboratives. Externalization, public accessibility, actual comprehension and opportunities to influence decisions are separate requirements; none establishes equitable outcomes by itself. This remains a proposal for discussion, not an adopted thesis or validated effect.
The author refines the concern toward methodological inspectability: a comparison between authorized water and water-budget components needs an explanation of how source records were processed and analyzed if others are to assess the comparison. The author reports being unable to locate the article’s methods; an exhaustive methods search has not been performed in this session.
The author proposes using the Draining Oregon example to explain why this transparency matters for public interpretation. A candidate narrative role is to move from the revised specification and explanatory artifacts to the public stakes of inspecting what a mapped comparison represents. The article presents a consequential public comparison; the checked memorandum supplies concrete reasons to ask how water-right records were counted, apportioned and interpreted. Together they motivate making the basis and limits of an interpretation available for scrutiny, without establishing an error in the article or a measured benefit from the proposed artifacts. Candidate claim WR-04 records this interpretive connection. The intended benefit is better grounds for informed assessment and disagreement; whether the artifacts achieve it remains to be evaluated.
Checked support: the October 29, 2021 OWRD Mid-Coast memorandum (midcoast-water-rights-memo-2021, methods on pages 3–4) documents difficulties using WRIS for regional/basin-scale analysis: counting and apportionment risks, permit conditions absent from database attributes, and differences between authorization and use. Its own regional analysis is presented with limitations. This is evidence that aggregation involves consequential interpretation, not that all spatial analysis is invalid. The later memorandum does not establish which problems occurred in the 2016 article. A defensible public-facing account can explain why the processing and interpretive choices need scrutiny while leaving the accuracy of that article’s calculations unresolved.
The author endorses the cleaner memorandum-based framing: it documents limitations encountered in OWRD technical assistance, and TAPs has deliberately sought to produce a useful dataset while incorporating the uncertainties associated with those limitations into the design of the dataset intended for the Oregon Open Data Portal. The memorandum establishes documented cautions in an earlier technical-assistance analysis; the description of TAPs’ deliberate response is author-reported. The revised specification remains to be inspected to establish how particular uncertainties are handled. A usable dataset can retain explicit limitations; neither their acknowledgment nor the planned publication establishes that every limitation is resolved.
This adds a substantive purpose to the proposed narrative’s third stage: the revision aims to carry learning and uncertainty into dataset design and public explanation. It is more than a change in documentation practice. Candidate claim WR-05 separates this reported design intent from the memorandum’s checked findings. Possible talk wording for author review: “Earlier technical-assistance work documented limitations in using these records. In TAPs, we are working to make a useful public dataset while carrying those limitations into its design and explanation.” Specific design treatments and outcomes remain to be checked.


Initial TAPs presentation
The initial presentation distinguishes proactive assistance from its report products (pages 3-5). Its capability staircase, production cycle and GenAI support areas serve different purposes; they do not establish completion. See the source assessment in the October 13 session.
The author clarifies that TAPs is transitioning from design to building, with incomplete staircase steps. This is an initial workflow account, not a final operating specification, despite the filename.

The author has assembled an evidence matrix from organizational files that traces a possible case arc: from schema and spatial attribution toward record meaning, the interpretation of query rows, translation between administrative and technical models, and questions of represented population and completeness. It may offer a concrete way to show how the questions changed, rather than making implementation detail the talk’s subject.

The source registry is unchanged, and no empirical or general benefit claim is established by this note.
The author also identifies Philosophy of Technology as a possible conceptual home for questions about technology, understanding, representation, assumptions, agency, and responsibility. This remains an emerging lens, not an adopted theory or a claim about what the literature establishes. The talk is not intended to be a philosophy lecture; any scholarly grounding should serve the practical case and be checked before use.

title: Frictionless Reasoning About a Resistant World
text:
A two-page guide

A readable draft still leaves questions about the circumstances its advice assumes.

Narrative:
Imagine we’re putting together a two-page water-conservation guide for communities experiencing water scarcity. We ask a bot for help, and soon we have something that reads pretty well. Two pages, clear headings, sensible-looking advice. But who does that advice imagine its readers to be? Do they own their homes? Can they control their water use? Can they afford the changes? Is it in a language and format they can use? The draft gives us somewhere to start. Those questions give us work to do.
Transition: The guide helps shape a relationship between people and the world. That brings us to mediation.
Support and boundaries: OP-01; author-approved hypothetical illustration.

title: Frictionless Reasoning About a Resistant World
text:
Technological mediation

Technologies help shape how we encounter and interpret the world.

Narrative:
That guide sits between people and something they’re trying to understand or act on. It selects what to include, what to emphasize, and how to explain it. This is what I mean by technological mediation: technologies help shape our relationships with the world. We can start with a very simple map—human, technology, world. In this example, the technology is the guide. As we look more closely, we begin to notice the choices inside what first looked like a straightforward connection.
Transition: Even this apparently simple relationship contains layers.

section: Onions and the work of scrutiny
text:
Onions and the work of scrutiny

Onions represent layered assumptions and conditions. Chopping represents scrutiny.

Narrative:
This is where I bring in the onions. At the center is the relationship as we first picture it: a person uses a guide. Around it are layers of assumptions and conditions. They’re there whether we look at them or not. Chopping is the work of looking closely. Think of getting onions ready for a salad bar. Somebody has to do the preparation. Not everybody volunteers. And sometimes there are tears. The questions are familiar: who does the work, who gets a say, and whose idea of a better salad are we working toward? For me, the metaphor makes room for effort and discomfort—and for asking how we share that work.
Transition: Now introduce the bot into developing the guide.
Support and boundaries: DR-02; author-defined metaphor and revised shading meaning, session 2026-10-28.

title: Frictionless Reasoning About a Resistant World
text:
The bot’s generative branch

We can question assumptions in a bot’s response without establishing, from the conversation alone, how they arose.

Narrative:
Let’s bring the bot into the picture. I’m working with it to develop the guide: asking questions, providing context, reading responses, making changes. Eventually, other people may use what we create. There’s another branch I want to draw from the bot: the generative process and the world its responses seem to assume. I call that represented world w-prime. Think of it as a question we can ask of an answer: what would have to be true for this advice to make sense? We can examine those assumptions. Establishing how they arose is harder. Asking the bot for an explanation gives us more words to examine; it doesn’t, on its own, establish their origin. Those vertical onions give us a particular challenge.
Transition: That limited visibility matters when the conversation feels easy to carry forward.

title: Frictionless Reasoning About a Resistant World
text:
Frictionless reasoning

A coherent draft can carry us forward before we examine whether its assumptions fit.

Narrative:
This is the tension behind frictionless reasoning. We have a coherent draft, the conversation is moving, and it’s easy to feel ready for the next step. Meanwhile, questions about affordability, control or access may still be waiting for us. The onions haven’t gone anywhere. We can bring some resistance into the process: check a record, ask someone with relevant experience, invite a different interpretation. Then we have choices about whose knowledge to bring in, what to question, and what to preserve. That unfolding process is what I want to share through my work.

title: Frictionless Reasoning About a Resistant World
text:
My work at OWRD

My technical-assistance work connects people and water data for planning.

Narrative:
I work at the Oregon Water Resources Department, OWRD. Part of my job is helping connect people with water data for planning. I think of technical assistance as working on that connection: what can these data help people understand, and what do people need in order to use them? Technical Assistance Packages—TAPs—is the work I’ll use to tell this story. We’re developing packages of analysis instructions, code and draft interpretations to support place-based water planning. There’s an ambitious direction here, and there are very practical questions about how we get there.
Transition: The TAPs direction changes how we are trying to make that assistance available.

Connecting people to data proactively

TAPs aims to make technical assistance available through open, reproducible products.

Narrative:
The direction is toward assistance that people can return to, examine and work with: moving from internal workflows toward reproducible work, and toward open, reproducible products. Reproducible means keeping the materials and steps needed to run the work again. As we develop that approach, I keep coming back to some practical questions. Who can we reach? When is the assistance available? Where does the work fall? And how does this change our connection with the people using it? Making something open is a step. Understanding what it takes for someone to use it gives us the next set of questions.
Transition: That ambition involves responsibilities across the product lifecycle.

title: Frictionless Reasoning About a Resistant World
text:
Can GenAI assist?

The work spans planning, design, implementation, testing, launch and user engagement.

Narrative:
As project lead, I have a hand in planning, design, implementation, testing, launch and engagement with users. There’s cross-division support, and much of the day-to-day development rests with me. So the question is very practical: can GenAI help us move this work forward with the capacity we have? It can help explore possibilities and put a strategy into words. But then I need to ask: whose working conditions does this strategy assume? Does it fit the people, time and support available here? That’s where the smooth conversation starts meeting the circumstances of the project.
Transition: I will walk through three touchpoints where that examination changed the work.

text:
Three touchpoints in an ongoing process

Planning, dataset design and implementation each introduce further equity questions.

Narrative:
I’ll take you through three touchpoints. First, planning: developing a longer-term vision and deciding what needs to happen today. Second, design: learning how to turn water-rights records into the public dataset we have in mind. Third, implementation: organizing the evolving work through a smart folder. In each one, we try an approach to a difficulty, and another set of questions comes into view. Follow the onions as we go.
Transition: Let us start with the longer-term vision—and what it asks of us today.

title: Frictionless Reasoning About a Resistant World
text:
Planning: a longer horizon

A long-term vision still requires choices about what to do now and whose capacity it assumes.

Narrative:
I wanted a longer-term vision: open data, work that people could run again, and eventually possibilities such as containerization. That means packaging software with its operating environment to help run it in a specified way. Then comes the question that brings a vision back to the desk: what do we need to do today? GenAI helped me explore that. Some plans also assumed data architects, dedicated IT support or established processes beyond my working setup. I kept bringing the conversation back to our circumstances. That was already resistance: asking the plan to meet the setting where we would actually have to carry it out.
Transition: Repeated conversations then raised a different problem: how to follow the reasoning across them.

section: Planning: bringing reasoning into a record
text:
Planning: bringing reasoning into a record

A durable record addressed tracing difficulties while creating selection decisions and documentation burden.

Narrative:
As the conversations accumulated, I started losing the thread. Which assumption came from which chat? What had we changed, and why? Sometimes a conversation would reach its limit while we were still working through something. I began moving selected reasoning into a durable record—files we could return to beyond an individual chat. That brought decisions into view: what deserves to stay, where does it go, and how do I explain it? Soon I also had a lot of documentation to look after. I was trying to build products, and keeping the record could become a job of its own. Preserving the reasoning gave me another set of onions to chop.
Transition: The design example shows why preserving a particular change in understanding can matter.

title: Frictionless Reasoning About a Resistant World
text:
WRIS: revising our understanding

Learning sessions changed what I thought the records could provide directly.

Narrative:
The Water Rights Information System, WRIS, gave me a concrete encounter with changing understanding. I initially expected information we could retrieve more directly. We had metadata listing variables that weren’t readily available through the records in the way I had pictured. Through learning sessions, I came to understand a historical family of connected records that needed careful translation. Imagine answering the latest email in a long thread. The answer depends on an attachment, which sends you to an older file, which points somewhere else. Suddenly, answering that top email takes more context than you expected. Colleagues helped me understand those connections. Some are approaching retirement, which adds urgency to the question of how that knowledge carries forward.
Transition: That learning changed what our specifications needed to explain.

title: Frictionless Reasoning About a Resistant World
text:
WRIS: preserving the translation decisions

GenAI helped document our evolving understanding and the decisions shaping revised specifications.

Narrative:
Those conversations with colleagues changed how I understood the records. I used GenAI to help follow that change and put it into words we could return to, including the comparison diagram. Our query specifications became more comprehensive and explicit about the steps toward the spatial dataset we want to offer publicly. I also moved toward folders organized around particular products, to keep documentation more focused. Now there’s another opportunity: share some of that developing understanding alongside the data, so people can examine the decisions shaping it. And another question: who gets to challenge that interpretation, and how? That includes our team and, eventually, the communities we hope will use the work.
Transition: How do we give that evolving record somewhere to live, and a way for others to work with it?
Support and boundaries: WR-02–WR-05; author-reported revised specifications, not an inspected artifact comparison or demonstrated improvement in community understanding.

title: Frictionless Reasoning About a Resistant World
text:
Implementation: a smart folder

The smart folder connects GenAI assistance with a durable record—and opens questions about access and participation.

Narrative:
The smart folder is one way I’m working on that connection. It’s a project folder with the work itself, instructions, sources, selected discussions, current understanding and decisions, linked together. This presentation project uses that structure. It gives GenAI assistance an interface with a record we can keep working on. Putting that record in a repository opens a possibility: other people could follow how assistance influenced development, and collaborators could keep accounts of their own assisted work. Then I have to ask: who can really get in? Who am I writing for? What skills and time do they need? An available repository gives us somewhere to begin those questions.
Transition: Making it available raises a further question: does participation require AI?
Support and boundaries: DR-06, TP-06; inspectable repository structure plus author-proposed collaborative use; no demonstrated access or accountability benefit.

title: Frictionless Reasoning About a Resistant World
text:
AI-assisted, not AI-dependent

People should be able to read, question and maintain the record without GenAI.

Narrative:
The principle is AI-assisted, not AI-dependent. People should be able to read, question and maintain the record without needing a model. We’re working with ordinary editable files, with instructions alongside them for assisted work. I’d also like that structure to travel across models, and perhaps eventually help us provide project context to a local language model. Another direction is a website that makes the record easier to navigate. Each of those choices asks something of the people using it. What do we expect them to know? What should be easy to find? How would they add a question or challenge an interpretation? The interface is another part of the equity work.
Transition: These approaches bring us back to the work of chopping.
Support and boundaries: TP-06–TP-07; design principle, existing editable files, and explicitly prospective interface/model ambitions. No tested accessibility or model portability claim.

title: Frictionless Reasoning About a Resistant World
section: How many onions are you willing to chop?
text:
How many onions are you willing to chop?

Scrutiny takes work. Who has the time, knowledge, access and authority to participate?

Narrative:
So, how many onions are you willing to chop? And perhaps more importantly: how much time, support and room do you have to do it? Across these examples, we’ve met assumptions about capacity, choices about what to document, changing interpretations of records, and questions about who can access the result. Even asking a team to review a draft leaves another question: can they see how it was generated and how their feedback shaped the next version? Participation can enter all along the way. Sharing that work means making room for people to question how the product is taking shape.
Transition: Our project-level relationships also sit within larger systems.
Support and boundaries: DR-07; author-directed normative questions and scope, not empirical findings about a community.
crumbs: Frictionless Reasoning About a Resistant World

title: Frictionless Reasoning About a Resistant World
text:
Our work within larger systems

Our project decisions sit within larger systems of power and influence.

Narrative:
Before closing, I want to acknowledge the larger picture. Our work sits within much larger systems of power and influence. People bring concerns about AI infrastructure, companies, public institutions and environmental consequences into these conversations. Those concerns deserve space. Today I’ve stayed close to decisions I encounter while developing a public-facing product. I’d like us to hold those scales together: keep the wider concerns in view while asking where we can act, question and change practice within our own organizations. For our discussion, how might those broader concerns connect to the choices we’ve been walking through?
Transition: Let me bring that back to the work we can keep doing together.
Support and boundaries: TP-08; author-proposed discussion framing. No quotations, factual assertions or identifying material from private event notes are reproduced.
crumbs: Frictionless Reasoning About a Resistant World

title: Frictionless Reasoning About a Resistant World
text:
Conclusion: keeping equity questions open

Each approach opens further equity questions. Productive resistance keeps them visible and open to participation as the work evolves.

Narrative:
What I hope this story leaves with you is a sense of the work continuing. I tried to preserve reasoning, and found questions about selection and burden. We documented a changing interpretation, and met questions about who could challenge it. We organized a repository, and opened questions about access and skills. Much of this has been a solo effort, and I want to find ways to bring others further into it. Productive resistance means keeping opportunities to question, learn and reconsider alive as we go. What makes that resistance productive is something we need to work out together, in the circumstances of each project. There will be more onions. The question is how we make room to chop them together.
Transition: Thank you. I look forward to continuing these questions in the shared Q&A at the end of the presentation cycle.
Support and boundaries: DR-08; author-directed conclusion checkpoint. Ready concerns the agreed framing, not empirical proof or completed participation.

title: Reproducibility notes
text:
Fresh clone
Install R and Quarto, open the .Rproj, and run renv::restore(). Then run quarto render from the repository root. The .Rprofile activates the project environment.

title: Reproducibility notes
text:
Build outputs
quarto render defaults to the complete profile. Its site is _site-complete/index.html; its deck is _site-complete/artifacts/talk/deck.html. The explicit command is quarto render --profile complete.
quarto render --profile focused builds the selected pages in _site-focused/, including its own copy of the deck. Both outputs are local and ignored. The earlier _site/ folder is legacy output, not updated by these profiles. No publication is part of the build.
Run quarto inspect . --profile complete or quarto inspect . --profile focused to inspect selections. The complete count grows with sessions and documentation; focused follows its explicit page list. Both run the same full provenance check during rendering. See the repository guide for maintaining selections and repository-link routing.

title: Reproducibility notes
text:
Updating and publishing site content
Edit source files, not generated copies in _site-complete/, _site-focused/ or the gh-pages branch. The focused profile is the routine review and publication build. The complete profile is a periodic comprehensive check; it does not need to be rendered after every focused-site change.

Updating existing files
For an existing page already selected by the focused profile, edit the source once and render focused:
quarto render --profile focused
This runs the full provenance check and refreshes the public-site candidate in _site-focused/. Existing supporting files such as CSS or images do not normally need their own project.render entries: a selected page or the project configuration incorporates or copies them when referenced. Confirm that new or changed assets are tracked, redistributable and outside ignored or restricted locations.
Review the rendered candidate through the repository’s static server:
./tools/serve-site.ps1 -Profile focused -Port 7188
Open http://localhost:7188/ for the site, http://localhost:7188/artifacts/talk/deck.html for the presentation and http://localhost:7188/docs/reproducibility-notes.html for these instructions. Stop the server with Ctrl+C. If port 7188 is already in use, choose another port and use that number in the URLs.
The server presents the existing _site-focused/ output over local HTTP, which is closer to GitHub Pages behavior than opening an HTML file directly from File Explorer. It allows relative links, scripts, search and copied assets to be checked without the browser restrictions and path differences associated with file:// URLs. Unlike quarto preview, this read-only server does not watch source files, display Quarto’s Render dialog or trigger another render during review. The files being reviewed therefore remain the exact publication candidate produced by the preceding focused render.
Check the landing page and focused navigation; the changed pages or slides; deck images, layout and transitions; Speaker View and notes using the S key; affected links and search results; and the absence of unintended, ignored or nonpublic files. Do not edit generated files to correct a problem: stop the server, edit the source, render focused again and repeat the review.
Render the complete profile periodically rather than as part of every routine edit:
quarto render --profile complete
Appropriate checkpoints include a broad project review or close-out, changes to complete-profile selection or navigation, adding or moving pages, reviewing unpushed edits to pages omitted from focused, and checking that the full knowledge base, sessions, documentation and deck still render together. An existing file shared by both profiles requires no profile-configuration change; each output reflects the edit the next time that profile is rendered.


Adding new files
For a new page, distinguish render selection from navigation. project.render determines whether Quarto creates the page. website.sidebar or website.navbar determines whether readers can discover it through site navigation. A rendered page may intentionally be absent from navigation when another page links to it directly.
The complete profile automatically selects Markdown files directly within knowledge-base/, sessions/ and docs/. Those patterns are not recursive and do not cover every directory or file type. Add an explicit entry to _quarto-complete.yml when a new page falls outside its existing patterns.
The focused profile is an explicit publication boundary. Add a new public page to project.render in _quarto-focused.yml, and add a sidebar or navbar entry when it should be discoverable through navigation. Render each affected profile once after adding or restructuring pages to verify its selection, navigation and links. Subsequent routine edits can return to the focused cadence above.
A link alone does not include its target in a profile. During a focused render, tools/focused-links.lua keeps local links to selected pages and redirects links to omitted Markdown pages to their source on the repository’s main branch. A redirected repository link does not make that page part of the GitHub Pages site.
New images, stylesheets and similar supporting assets normally belong in a tracked source location and are referenced by an included page or configuration; they do not normally belong in project.render. After rendering, verify that they appear in every intended output and that no ignored, nonpublic or restricted material was copied.


Commit and publish
After reviewing the affected output, inspect the source changes and exclusions:
git status --short
git diff --check
git diff
Stage explicit source and provenance files, inspect the staged diff, and commit only with the author’s authorization. Do not stage _site-focused/, _site-complete/, private notes, data, source PDFs or unrelated working files. Use the commit convention in the repository guide. Pushing main requires separate explicit authorization.
After an authorized source push and a successful focused render, publish the exact reviewed focused output only with separate publication authorization:
quarto publish gh-pages --profile focused --no-render
The --no-render option prevents publication from silently rebuilding the candidate after review. Quarto updates and pushes the dedicated gh-pages branch; _site-complete/ remains a local review output and is not published. Confirm the new gh-pages build, open the public landing page and affected URLs, verify key assets and deck behavior, review Git status again, and record the result in the dated session.
